title: Harvard plates show partial eclipses of HD 303514 from 1910 to 1956 at a near-constant depth, which a constant inclination drift does not explain
abstract: HD 303514 is a twin eclipsing binary (P = 19.897 d) whose eclipses became shallower from 2002 to 2026. Published models fit to these years predict eclipse loss near 2030. We used 1,475 Harvard DASCH plates from 1889 to 1990 to test the eclipse history 100 years further back. One eclipse ephemeris and one twin-star template fit five plate eras together. The coherent statistic is 63.2, against at most 50.8 for 300 wrong periods (p = 0.003) and 18 to 37 for eight comparison stars. An independent plate calibration gives 83.7. The impact parameter was almost constant from 1910 to 1956: 0.59, 0.37, 0.61 and 0.52 in four eras (1-sigma ranges 0.05 to 0.13). The 91 plates of 1969-1990 show no eclipse (b > 0.58 at 2 sigma). In simulations with the real plate noise, the published linear drift fails (p = 0.001; p = 0.011 with the 1889-1956 plates only), because it gives no eclipses before 1912 and deep eclipses later. A fixed-axis precession with a nodal period of 263-331 yr fits the modern depths and the 1889-1956 plates. It predicts central eclipses near 1979, which the 1969-1990 plates do not show (p = 0.008). Two constant eclipsing binaries show that the plates do not compress eclipse amplitudes. Thus the present inclination change did not continue at a constant rate for the full century. The eclipse loss near 2030 remains likely, but we cannot give a reliable return date. Limits: a simple twin-disc model, few plates near the eclipse phases in 1969-1990, no plates from 1956 to 1969, and no spectroscopic orbit of the third body.
